newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: NETHERLANDS TO LAUNCH CAMPAIGN ON GENETICALLY-ENGINEERED SOYBEANS.
newsitem.headline: NETHERLANDS TO LAUNCH CAMPAIGN ON GENETICALLY-ENGINEERED SOYBEANS.

text.p: The Netherlands said on Wednesday it would launch a campaign over the coming months to inform the public over the controversial import of new genetically-engineered soybeans from the United States.
"You have to be open about this and tell the consumer that this type of soybean is coming into Europe," agriculture minister Jozias van Aartsen told a press briefing.
But he said the Dutch would not ban the U.S. product despite opposition from consumer and environmental groups.
The so-called transgenic soybeans have been genetically altered to withstand treatment by the herbicide Roundup.

The technology was developed by U.S. chemicals giant Monsanto, which forecasts farmers in the United States will plant five to ten million acres of the beans this autumn, up to around one sixth of the total crop.
Monsanto says the new beans require treatment from fewer herbicides than normal, because Roundup controls a greater variety of weeds than competing products.

But environmental lobby group Greenpeace, which opposes genetic engineering alleging it promotes allergies, says the consumer will have no choice in whether or not to eat the new beans, which will find their way into a wide variety of foods.
Van Aartsen said there were no risks associated with the new technology.
"We have looked at it in depth and we say there is no problem at all with this soybean," he said.
But he acknowledged the labelling question was problematic and said it was impossible to separate modified and non-modified beans.
"You can't tell exactly where modified soybeans have been used. It vanishes into the whole (food) chain. This is why you should tell the consumer it (the technology) is there."

Last week, Chicago Board of Trade Chairman Patrick Arbor said the exchange would accept transgenic soybeans for delivery against CBOT futures contracts. --Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000, Fax +31 20 504 5040
